name: Fisherman's Wharf
summary_en: Fisherman's Wharf is a district rather than a building, and its record is a long argument about whether it is a working harbour or a destination. The Port's 1981 Action Plan, prepared by ROMA, framed the problem: tenants wanted restrooms, sidewalk treatment, parking management and rubbish disposal, and the plan insisted that for the area to keep its tourist appeal "the authenticity of maritime activity" had to be maintained. A 1986 management audit by the Board of Supervisors' Budget Analyst found the Port could not say what the wharf cost it — it did not know the maintenance costs of either Fisherman's Wharf or Pier 94/96 — while carrying $3.68 million of delinquent tenant accounts. The Port's own 1987 staff report on commercial fishing facilities carried a consultant's assessment of what the fleet and the fish handlers needed, developed with wharf tenants and adopted by the Commission in 1986. That work ended in the Hyde Street Fishing Harbor, whose environmental report the City Planning Commission certified in December 1996; the comments on the draft include a speaker describing thirty fishing boats "tied up helter skelter in the outer lagoon with no water, no power, no toilets". Recorded contract payments against the wharf as a whole are negligible, because Port work is contracted pier by pier rather than by district.

As a center of the commercial fishing industry, and second largest tourist attraction in the State, it plays a vital role within the City. However, the Wharf has begun to show signs of over- commercialization, that threatens its appeal and eco- nomic well-being. At the same time, the fishing in-

cal facilities. Concerns have been voiced by many port tenants that public improvements, such as restrooms, sidewalk treatment, parking management and trash disposal are needed. Increasingly, tenants have requested changes of use and alterations to long-term leases, raising questions about the future of the area. Despite its difficulties, Fisherman's Wharf continues as a viable center for fish handling and dis- tribution. The fishing industry is important, not only for the jobs that it creates, but also as an attractive setting for tourism. To continue its tourist appeal, the authenticity of maritime activity must be ensured. Further, if Wharf businesses are to be successful, seasonal peaks n

be leveled out throughout the year, by attracting residents as well as tourists. This will, in turn, depend upon the improvement of the present public environment as wel] as the maintenance of the traditional maritime role of the Wharf. The recommendations of the Action Plan, therefore, are to maintain and enhance the fishing industry at Fisherman's Wharf, with the construction of the new Hyde Street Pier. Further, changes of use within Fish Alley will be restricted to continued fish hand- ling use. Necessary improvements to wharves and fac- ilities are also proposed. There is great opportunity for the 1l-acre Pier 45 to improve access and views to the bay, as well as to complement existing uses at the Wharf.
